subject: capybaraOnsen
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: capybaras in a hot spring.
Style: kawaii.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a kawaii capybara hot spring diorama as a single TypeScript module, sketching the structure: a rock-rimmed oval pool with water surface and rising steam, built through a scene builder API.

Since each rigged model only allows one root joint, I'm designing a shared "root" joint for the diorama with individual capybara skeletons (hips, etc.) parented to it. I'm writing a helper function that builds each capybara's joints in local model space, applying rotation, scaling, and translation so multiple capybaras can be placed and oriented independently, and now I'm working out realistic body proportions and scale for the creatures.

Now I'm thinking through the pool diorama: setting water and floor heights so capybaras sit submerged to mid-body with their lowest points resting on the pool bottom, and designing the basin with a grassy base disc, scattered rock clusters around the rim, and an opaque turquoise water layer rather than using transparency.

I'm settling the vertical layout: the dirt/grass base runs y 0 to 0.1, with the pool basin floor at y=0.1 where capybaras sit, rim rocks rising to 0.45, and water surface around 0.35 so bodies stay partly submerged while heads clear it. That puts the diorama's total height near 0.7 with capybara heads at the top, plus steam rising above.

I'm also planning small props now—a glowing stone lantern beside the pool, a bamboo spout feeding water in, floating yuzu fruits with tiny leaves, maybe a wooden bucket and a folded towel. For the capybaras, I'm picturing three: a big adult with a yuzu balanced on its head and happy closed eyes, a second adult wearing a folded towel on its head, and a small baby perched on one of their backs.

I'm sketching the capybara's body proportions and sitting pose, keeping in mind that the legs will mostly be hidden underwater, so the rest pose just needs to read clearly for rigging purposes.

Settling on body center at y=0.27 so it's half-submerged in the water, since the water disc will just intersect the mesh naturally. Now I'm starting to lay out the skeleton hierarchy per capybara, beginning with the hips joint parented to root.

Naming joints uniquely per capybara using a suffix, then defining the spine chain from hips to chest, and a neck/head chain with a large rounded head for a kawaii look. I'm considering using a sweep along the spine bones rather than separate chain-plus-mesh to build the body shape.

For the actual implementation, I'll make hips the explicit root joint, then build a spine chain over a catmull path with one joint per span between points -- so four control points give three named spine joints parented to hips.

For the body shape, I'm sweeping that spine chain with a radius function returning slightly wider-than-tall ellipses (rx around 0.19-0.23, ry around 0.19-0.23) that taper toward the rump and front, giving the capybara its characteristic barrel-shaped torso.

For coloring, I'm defining a mottled warm brown coat (#b57d45/#a06c3a) with a lighter countershaded belly (#e2b886) for that classic capybara look, and considering whether to apply toon-kit cel shading for a kawaii hard-shadow aesthetic since the fixed-light approach should work fine given the model's rotation.

I'm weighing whether to pull in the toon kit's cel, INK, furEdge, and glow utilities versus hand-rolling my own paints and eyes—glow matters for the lantern effect so I'll import that, and cel shading seems safe to layer on top of the mottled fur paint. Writing fur and belly blending logic...

Now shifting to the capybara's head geometry: boxy rounded snout, bulbous nose, small round ears set back, eyes placed high and forward-facing for the kawaii look, starting with a scaled sphere for the skull base.

For the nose, I'm planning a small dark brown oval nub at the top-front of the muzzle, kawaii-style with nostrils and a highlight. The mouth gets a tiny "w" decal, and I'm splitting the jaw into an upper part fixed on the head and a lower jaw part attached at a separate joint so it can move.

For facial decals, I'm placing pink cheek blush ellipses and eye textures (dot eyes with highlights, happy arc eyes, sleepy curved eyes) directly onto the skull sphere's surface using decal projection with position and direction parameters to wrap them naturally around the curved head.

Actually, since word directions are in model axes, yaw rotation breaks that for rotated capybaras. I should instead pass a yaw quaternion directly to the part so mesh scale applies in local space before rotation, keeping axes consistent with the capybara's own orientation.

Writing helper functions for position and direction transforms...

For the body construction, I'll avoid skin-surface calculations for complexity and just place decals and features using direct world-space points computed from the yaw-rotated P function. I'm figuring out leg proportions for the capybara standing in the basin—body center around y=0.29 with radius 0.22 puts the belly near 0.07, so legs need to span roughly that height.

Front legs run from shoulder points down to foot points with a slight backward elbow bend; hind legs similarly run from hip to foot with a forward knee bend, using two-bone limb chains (shoulder, elbow, hand / hip, knee, foot) swept with tapering radii. I'm adding small flattened toe spheres at each foot tip, darker in color to suggest hooves.

Now I'm working out the ground layout: a base cylinder covers everything at y=0..0.1 in a stone/soil tone with the pool floor and surrounding ground both sitting at y=0.1, topped with a flat grass ring (a lathe shape) between radius 1.75 and 2.2, and a ring of rim rocks around radius 1.65 to frame the basin.

I'm making the pool and base slightly elliptical for a more natural diorama look — scaling the water disc and rock placements along x and z (roughly 1.7 by 1.35), and shaping the base slab as an oval with a beveled lathe profile rather than a perfect circle.

Rather than fighting with lathe scaling, I'll just use a simple cylinder geometry stretched into an ellipse via non-uniform scale for both the soil base and a thin grass layer on top, then place the elliptical water disc on top of that at the right height.

I'll center the water cylinder at y=0.255 with a ripple decal on top, surround the pool with a grass ring and rim rocks, and then scale up a lantern around 0.9-1m tall placed at the back-right to anchor the overall composition.

For the water, I'm going for a milky turquoise tone with mottled paint shading for subtle color variation, then adding a ripple texture made from concentric rings and highlights on a scaled ellipse plane facing upward.

For the steam, I'm using wispy upright card sprites with crossed geometry positioned above the pool, rendered with alpha-tested white translucent puff shapes to suggest soft rising steam.

I'm adding floating yuzu citrus as small flattened spheres with tiny leaf accents scattered on the water surface, and considering a small wooden bucket lathe shape with banded rim detail to float nearby.

I'll lay the hoops flat using a torus geometry rotated into the right plane. For the stone lantern, I'm planning a granite-colored base, pillar, glowing fire box with orange light, hexagonal roof, and finial sphere, then moving on to a jointed bamboo spout angled to pour water into the pool.

Now I'm positioning the bamboo pipe emerging from a small rock pile at the back-left, with a pale blue-white water stream falling from its tip into the pool and creating a ripple ring at the splash point.

For the rim, I'm scattering 22 faceted low-poly rocks around the pool ellipse using a randomized placement, with a greyish-lavender pastel palette and a mottled paint texture to give them a soft stone look.

Writing rock paint function...

The rocks need to stay clear of the capybaras' cleared central area, so they ring the perimeter instead.

I'm settling on around 8-9 textures to cover the various decorative elements, each carrying its own colors. Now I'm moving onto capybara anatomy, starting with small rounded ears at the back of the head, scaled slightly larger than realistic for a kawaii look, with pink inner detail positioned near the top of the head.

Working out local coordinates for the capybara: forward is +Z, up is +Y, with the body curving from z≈-0.36 to 0.30 and the head sitting low at around y=0.42, scaled up for a big-headed kawaii proportion. I'm defining skull and muzzle dimensions and their center points to build the head shape.

Now I'm placing the nose nub, upper lip divide, and lower jaw as separate shapes, planning to decal a simple smile texture onto the front of the muzzle. I'm also starting to position the eyes high and wide on the sides of the skull to keep that kawaii look.

I'm checking whether the muzzle sphere might visually overlap or hide the eye decal near x=.095, since the muzzle's surface extends close to where the eye sits at z≈.64, but since decals project only onto their designated target surface, muzzle occlusion shouldn't actually affect the eye placement unless it physically covers that area.

To avoid any z-fighting, I'm shrinking the muzzle radius to 0.1 and nudging the eye position to x=.108, y=.455, confirming this keeps the eyes outside the muzzle's bounds while landing correctly on the skull surface at z≈.626. I'm also considering restructuring the head coordinates around a local head-center reference point to simplify future offset calculations, then placing the cheek blush decals symmetrically near the lower cheeks.

I'm skipping eyebrows for a cleaner kawaii look, but adding thin whisker rods on each side of the muzzle for detail, computed as small spikes radiating outward in a dark color. I'm also sketching in two tiny white buck-tooth rectangles peeking out just under the upper lip for a playful capybara touch.

Positioning the teeth boxes near the jaw area, accepting some slight embedding since the lower jaw sphere overlaps that region. For the ears, I'm placing scaled, outward-tilted spheres on each side of the head with smaller pink inner-ear spheres offset in front, using yaw-only rotation to preserve the tilt.

I'm adding a helper function for combined rotations, then designing hat props: an orange yuzu citrus sphere on the head, and a folded towel box with painted blue stripes, both positioned near the top of the head. I'm also sketching out eye variants (open dot, happy curved, sleepy curved) as SVG shapes, and noting capybaras lack a visible tail, just a small rear nub to rig.

I'm planning the skeleton joint hierarchy per capybara—spine chain, neck, head, jaw, shoulders—using a naming convention with suffixes per character to keep chains distinct for the rigger.

Now I'm plotting the actual spine point positions building the hips-to-spine chain upward and forward, then continuing into the neck chain connecting the spine's end to the head base.

Defining the head joint attached to the neck's last segment, then thinking through whether the body sweep needs separate coverage for the neck region.

Defining smooth sine-based profile functions...

Checking proportions: body spans roughly -0.5 to 0.5 in length with the head centered at 0.52, overlapping the chest slightly, which should look fine. I'll bump sweep tessellation sides to 10 for a smoother low-poly look, use cel shading with key light in model space for the coat, and let the pale belly show through via normal-based fur edges — skipping cheek fur tufts for now but considering a few small kawaii details as signature touches.

For those kawaii touches, I'll add a pink nose, blush, shiny eyes, a hat, little feet, and a small ahoge tuft on the head made from three leaf-shaped extrusions. I'm skipping the belly water ring idea, and for baby capybaras I'll scale everything down to 0.55 with a head-boost factor so heads stay proportionally bigger — defining offsets relative to the head center scaled by that boost parameter.

Setting up the capybara helper function with position, yaw, scale, eye style, and hat options...

Each sphere part gets a fresh low-poly geometry, and painting works in model space after the transform is applied. I'm defining the rotation as a yaw quaternion combined with per-part Euler rotations, then starting to lay out the head parts with their bone attachments and dimensions, like the skull ellipsoid sized relative to head height.

Working through the muzzle and nose placement next, computing their offsets and sizes relative to the skull so the face proportions stay kawaii-style, with slightly different coat tones for the muzzle and a darker pink-brown for the nose.

Still placing facial features...

I'll place the mouth decal slightly lower, around y -0.06, z 0.237, to sit under the muzzle tip near the teeth. For the eyes, I'm computing where the eye decals should sit on the skull surface using the skull's ellipsoid radii, landing on roughly hp(s*0.115, 0.03, 0.125).

Checking for overlap between the eye decals and the muzzle sphere at this position, I find the overlap region is small enough to ignore, so I'll nudge the eyes slightly higher and outward to hp(s*0.12, 0.05, 0.115).

Now I'm adding blush marks and working out the ear geometry - ellipsoids positioned on the top-back of the head with flattened proportions and a tilt rotation, plus smaller inner-ear pink ellipsoids placed just forward of them.

For the forehead I'm sketching a small tuft using spike cones angled forward from the top of the head in a darker brown, then starting on a yuzu-colored hat ellipsoid positioned above the head.

Adding leaf and towel accessories...

Now I'm placing the feet with small hoof-colored toe ellipsoids positioned so they touch the floor, then adjusting leg sweep radii for the chain.

I'm adding a tiny tail stub joint parented to the hips with a small dark sphere, then setting up whisker spikes as thin tapered cylinders positioned along the snout with varying direction and length.

For the eyes, I'm drawing an SVG texture with a dark iris ellipse, a brownish inner iris, and two white highlight circles to give a glossy, lifelike look.

For the expressions, I'm sketching happy eyes as a curved smiling stroke, sleepy eyes as a downward curve with small lash ticks, and blush as a pink ellipse with faint hatch lines, making sure the textures stay transparent outside the shapes with alpha testing.

Now I'm adding the mouth as a wavy "w" path in dark stroke, then thinking about kawaii extras like floating pink hearts above the happy capybara for extra charm.

I'm also adding sparkle textures alongside hearts, bringing the total texture count to around eleven, then working out the exact placement of a stone lantern near the rim, checking its coordinates against the elliptical pool and grass boundaries to make sure it sits correctly outside the rim edge.

Now I'm roughing out the lantern's construction: a hexagonal base cylinder, a narrower pillar, and a wider plinth, stacking their heights.

Still writing lantern geometry...

Working out the lantern's total height budget across its segments, then thinking about how to texture the glow window with a warm gradient and dark crossbar frame to give it that paper-lantern look.

Now I'm planning extra kawaii details: yuzu floating in the bucket, and a small wooden tray bobbing on the water carrying tiny cups and a sake bottle. I'm also starting to lay out the capybaras' positions around the pool's elliptical shape.

Working through capybara placement—the big happy adult near (-0.5,-0.1) facing inward, a sleepy adult with a towel on the opposite side facing back toward the first, and a baby capybara near the front center with a small heart bubble instead of a hat, plus the floating tray positioned nearby.

Checking if the baby's head and body placement near the pool edge overlaps with the adult heads — seems like there's enough gap, so I'll nudge the baby slightly right rather than attempt something like perching it on A's back, which feels overly complex.

I'm verifying the pool boundary math to make sure the baby's head stays submerged within the water radius, then checking that the front rim rocks are low enough not to block the viewer's sightline to the capybaras — I'll vary rock heights so the front ones sit lower. With the camera facing forward, the composition should read correctly. Now I'm positioning the five floating yuzu citrus spheres around the water surface, and starting to lay out the tray dimensions.

Still writing lathe geometry...

Steam should stay mostly hidden behind and at the edges of the capybaras rather than in front, so I'm placing wisps with narrower heights toward the back half and sides so they don't obscure the animals. For grass tufts, I'm positioning small three-blade clusters along the ring between the rocks and the grass edge, scaling their radius to fit that boundary.

I'm placing small stick-stemmed five-petal flowers around the same ring, counting up the full texture list (eyes, blush, mouth, ripple, steam, tuft, flower, heart, sparkle, window) to confirm I'm within budget. I also realize all the scenery cards need an explicit root bone assignment since they currently default to no joint.

Setting up a single root joint at the origin for everything to bind to, then placing heart cards above the happy capybara's head using its head-top position as reference. I'm checking that symmetric decorations like hearts and sparkles will read correctly regardless of viewing direction, since the flow orientation flips how asymmetric cards appear from front versus back.

Deciding flow:[0,0,1] so flowers and tufts face correctly when viewed from downstream, using cross:true for most elements but no cross for flowers since they're viewed edge-on. For glow effects, I'll wrap the heart card meshes with glow(), and I'm now working out the bamboo spout as a tilted six-sided cylinder rod.

Sketching bamboo node rings at a few points along the spout using small flat cylinders oriented along the pipe direction, plus a darker cap disc to close off the open end.

Now I'm adding the water stream geometry dropping from the spout to the basin, a thin flat-ended rod with a light blue color, along with a flat splash ring and bubble detail at the surface. Then I'm placing a trio of rocks near the spout base at varying heights to form a support pile.

I'm checking that these rocks fall within the base ellipse and align with the rim boundary so the larger rocks naturally blend with the rim edge, then positioning the pipe's back end to rest on top of the tallest rock near y≈0.7-0.77, adjusting for slight embedding.

For rock geometry, I'm weighing low-poly icosahedron detail levels for a crystalline look, and since the geometry is non-indexed with duplicate vertices per face, I need a jitter function based on rounded vertex position (not index) so shared vertices move together and avoid visible cracks between faces.

Now I'm doing a budget check: part counts stay under 1000 across capybaras, rocks, and texture cards, color palette stays around 25 flat tones, and triangle counts from spheres and other geometry should land safely under the 60k limit.

I'm reviewing the toon and glow kit imports to confirm they're correct, then double-checking the part API signature—specifically whether scale accepts a number or needs to be passed as a vector array.

Checking how decal targets and chain paths work, since decals need a valid surface target and chains take a path input that could be a catmull curve through points.

For the leg structure, I'm thinking through using a limb function that returns joint points, then feeding those into a chain with a parent bone and matching names array, keeping it anchored off the mid-plane.

For bends, I'm working out whether to pass a single direction vector or a list with one element for the inner elbow joint, since the API seems to accept either form but it's ambiguous which shape is expected here.

Now I'm sketching the leg geometry: computing shoulder-to-foot and hip-to-foot distances to confirm the segment lengths reach the targets, then deciding elbow and hock bend directions (back-facing) for front and hind legs respectively.

For side naming I'm just checking x-position determines "L" or "R" labels, though yaw rotation means the actual side could shift—not critical here. Then I'm setting up the leg sweeps with tapered radii following each joint chain to form the coat shape.

Neck and body sweeps use similar circular cross-sections, with the body adding a sides parameter for mesh resolution; none of this needs pose adjustments. Parts reference bones like the head joint directly, and rotations combine yaw and local Euler angles into quaternions for proper orientation. I'm now checking what parameters the part-attachment function accepts.

Setting up imports for the builder utilities and toon/glow kits, then defining the scene metadata for a capybara onsen scene.

Writing vector and quaternion helpers...

I'm checking that cel's lit paint gets resolved recursively so nested colors work correctly, and that the shadow side derives its hue by darkening whatever the lit color resolves to.

Now I'm defining the color palette for the character's features—muzzle, cream, nose, ears, feet, tufts—along with accent colors like yuzu and leaf, each wrapped in cel() to produce resolvable paints. I'm also sketching out the hot spring scene's water texture using a mottled teal gradient before moving on to the soil coloring.

Writing cylinder geometry code...

Now I'm placing rim rocks in a loop around the pool, jittering their angle and radius, scaling them down and flattening the front-facing ones so they sink lower near the viewer, with their tops settling just above the water line.

Checking rock heights against the water level confirms they sit comfortably above it, and the capybara head position still clears everything. I'm working out the rocks' x-span so they overlap slightly into the water without looking wrong, then setting up the rocks as jittered, non-uniformly scaled icosahedra with flat shading, moss-colored tops in a pastel lavender-green palette.

Now I'm defining the capybara builder function, working out the type signature for eyes and hats, and figuring out how to type the joint parameter using a return-type trick off the builder instead of importing types directly. Writing capybara body construction...

Defining a head-level ellipsoid shorthand, then setting up the skeleton joints starting with the hips as the root spine joint.

Still building the spine chain with catmull-rom control points...

Adding the jaw joint off the head with an aim offset, then setting up the body sweep along the spine with a coat-colored, ten-sided profile.

Now I'm defining the neck sweep with its own radius profile, checking that the cap ends are hidden properly at the head and body joints. For the legs, I'm looping over left and right sides, building front limb points from hip to paw positions and verifying the reach distance against the scaled limb lengths.

Setting up the arm chain with named joints for shoulder, elbow, and hand, parented to the spine, then sweeping a tapered radius along it and placing an elliptical foot shape with three small toe nubs at the tip. Now I'm starting on the hind limb points, defining the hip and ankle target positions scaled similarly to the front legs.

Working through the leg chain naming and parenting it to the hips joint instead of the spine, with a thicker thigh radius tapering down, and confirming the leg geometry stays mostly hidden below the body or underwater so visibility isn't a concern. Then I move on to planning the tail joints and ellipse shapes, followed by whiskers, and finally the eye textures and decal sizing system that references dot, happy, sleep, blush, and mouth textures scaled by the character's overall size.

Now I'm computing precise decal placement for eyes, mouth, nose, and teeth — checking that each decal's position lands close to its parent surface (muzzle, nose sphere) using normalized distance math, and adjusting the mouth and teeth vertical offsets so they align under the nose without overlapping incorrectly.

I'm also figuring out jaw geometry: since the default jaw placement sits hidden inside the muzzle, I'm shifting its center lower so part of it protrudes visibly as a chin beneath the muzzle.

Now I'm positioning hat elements on the skull: the yuzu citrus piece, leaves, and a towel wrapped around the head using a flattened box with stripe paint, plus considering an ellipsoid roll for the towel's top edge.

I also want a small ahoge tuft when no hat is present, and I'm deciding to skip cheek ruffs to keep things simple. Finally I'm planning to have the capybara function return reference points like head top position for things like floating hearts to use.

Now I'm sketching the scenery helpers (yuzu float, bucket, lantern, tray, spout) and working through the card SDK API, placing textured cards using frame positions and directions, keeping color tinting off so the texture's own colors show. I'm designing simple SVG textures for the flower (stem, petals, center) and the tuft (blade shapes) to attach to these cards.

Designing steam, heart, sparkle, and ripple SVG textures...

Working out the water decal plane geometry and sizing it to match the ring proportions, then setting up the plane's orientation and up-axis for correct placement.

For the lantern's window texture, I'm sketching a gradient-filled rect with a warm yellow-orange glow and considering adding a crescent moon cutout detail.

Now I'm setting up a helper function for scenery parts attached to the root bone, and thinking through bone orientation for shapes like the torus using direction and axis parameters.

Checking that position lands outside the rocks but within the grass area, confirming it's fine for the bucket with the towel and yuzu fruits inside. I'm building the bucket as a lathe shape in wood tones with two small spheres for yuzu resting at floor height, then setting up torus hoops with radius varying by height for the bucket's metal bands.

Verifying the lathe outline for the bucket traces a clean loop from the outer bottom edge up the outer wall, across the rim, down the inner wall, and back along the axis without self-intersecting. Now I'm placing the stone lantern at a chosen spot near the rocks and starting to write the lantern construction function.

Building lantern base, pillar, cap, and glowing window geometry...

Roofs get mossy coloring based on normal direction, and I'm planning steam wisps for the pool with randomized placement, plus floating heart frames positioned above capybara A's head at varying offsets and sizes, with sparkles near B and the baby. Now I'm starting the final build function, setting up the builder and root joint.

Writing root joint and rock geometry...

Now I'm placing steam card particles rising from the water surface with randomized positions and curling bend, then moving on to scatter grass tufts in a ring pattern around the scene.

I'll add a second batch of flowers with a different random seed around the same ellipse region, keeping grass sparse near the bucket and lantern props. I'm also double-checking that head decals correctly inherit yaw orientation and that the decal's up-vector defaults to world +Y, then setting up small floating sphere elements for each position.

Now I'm defining wood grain coloring for props, then placing the two adult figures and the baby with specific positions, scales, yaw rotations, and poses (happy/yuzu, sleep/towel, and a slightly turned baby with a dot expression), working out the baby's head offset relative to its body scale.

Checking that all the figures stay within the water boundary and that their head positions don't collide with each other or the rocks, calculating the gap between figure A and figure B's heads to confirm adequate spacing, and considering whether a tray prop can fit in the remaining space between the two bodies without overlapping.

Writing ear rotation logic...

Assembling the final build, defining helper types for the builder, joints, and texture sets before writing out the complete TypeScript code.

Now designing the eye SVGs, laying out iris and pupil shapes with ellipses and circles to get the right highlight placement, checking the geometry stays within bounds.

Next I'm writing a rock paint function that blends base colors with noise and adds moss patches using smoothstep thresholds on height and texture.

I still need to verify the paint function returns a valid color type, add subtle shading, check wood grain details, ensure unique naming across generated parts, and finalize capybara eye positioning. I also want to confirm the lantern cylinder geometry helper and array-based position arguments are correct before writing the final answer.

Checking sweep radius chains, leg and neck limb geometry, head joint orientation vectors, and confirming the limb import path from the SDK. I'm also verifying the water decal plane with ripple texture and the sparkle/heart frame orientation, then writing everything out while double-checking the yuzu bucket placement.

Finalizing with a generic blob sphere helper, segmented water cylinder painting, and heart card sizing before locking in the final code.
